name: Dragon's blood resin

card.summary: A deep-red plant resin from several tropical trees, used in folk medicine and some Korean and natural skincare for wound-healing and skin-soothing claims.
card.aka: Sangre de drago, sangre de grado
card.note: Source species differ (Croton, Dracaena, Calamus); Calamus resin has been described as anticoagulant.

quick.overview:
Dragon's blood is a bright red resin or latex tapped from different trees, including Croton lechleri in the Amazon, Dracaena species on Socotra and the Canary Islands, and rattan palms. It has long been used as a dye, varnish, incense and folk remedy, and today appears in some skincare for soothing and healing skin.

The appearance angle is skin recovery: users apply it hoping for calmer, quicker-healing skin and fewer marks. Laboratory and small clinical work covers wound healing and antimicrobial activity, while reviews say dermatology uses need further study.
quick.how: It is used as a topical latex or resin extract, or as an ingredient in creams and Korean-style cosmeceuticals. It is applied to small cuts, irritated skin or marks. People often add it to a normal routine; results are described over days to weeks.
quick.risks: Reported topical side effects are limited in the literature, but the plant species varies by product. Calamus-derived resin has been described as anticoagulant. A rat study of a Dracaena extract found it tolerated at high oral amounts. Patch testing and checking the species are common cautions.

lead: Dragon's blood is the name for several bright red tree resins or latexes used since antiquity as varnish, pigment, incense and medicine [6]. In appearance and skincare, the Amazonian sangre de drago (Croton lechleri) and Dracaena resins are used topically in the hope of faster-healing, calmer skin [1][2].

The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea mentions Socotra as a source in the 1st century, and Greeks, Romans and Arabs used it medicinally; medieval writers invented dragon and elephant origin stories [6]. In the Amazon, Indigenous peoples have applied Croton lechleri latex to cuts, bites and blisters, where it dries into a 'second skin' [7].

Research includes laboratory and animal studies of anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and antimicrobial effects and small clinical studies of wound healing; a 2019 dermatology review concluded the plant has limited current dermatologic use and needs further investigation [4]. A 2020 review lists dragon's blood among bioactive ingredients in Korean cosmeceuticals [1].

chain: Forms a protective layer; claimed wound-healing and anti-inflammatory action
angle.text: People apply dragon's blood to cuts, blemishes and irritated skin, aiming for quicker healing and a calmer complexion. The proposed benefit rests on traditional use and lab data, with limited clinical testing.

paras: Several unrelated trees yield red resins sold as dragon's blood: Calamus rattan palms (the main commercial source), Dracaena trees from the Canary Islands, Morocco and Socotra, Croton trees in South America, and Pterocarpus [6]. Croton lechleri resin is mainly proanthocyanidins, with taspine as the identified wound-healing component in animal models [7]. A Planta Medica review of C. lechleri covers phytochemicals and pharmacology across 33 articles [2].

The resin served as a violin varnish in 18th-century Italy, a pigment in art, a colorant for Chinese furniture and New Year paper, and in religious ceremonies in India [6]. Balfour's 1880 expedition to Socotra led to the first scientific study of its origin, and it was sold as a cure-all between 1880 and 1914 [6]. Socotran locals have used Dracaena resin for wounds and skin disorders such as eczema [6]. A 2008 ethnopharmacology review describes uses as hemostatic, antimicrobial and wound healing [5].

A 2020 review of bioactive ingredients in Korean cosmeceuticals lists dragon's blood, alongside snail mucin and bee venom, as an ingredient with potential skin-rejuvenation, photoprotection and wound-healing applications, and says further research is warranted [1]. Users apply it to small wounds, marks and irritated skin.

Evidence is mostly preclinical. A 2019 review found anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antimicrobial and antiviral effects in preclinical work, with clinical studies reflecting wound-healing and antiviral properties, and concluded dermatologic use is limited and needs more study [4]. A 2025 review reached similar conclusions on wound-healing and other activity [2]. The purified oligomer crofelemer from the sap has clinical data in diarrhea and was FDA-approved in 2013 [7].

A 2018 rat study found a Dracaena cinnabari extract tolerated at high oral amounts in acute and sub-acute tests [6]. Calamus resin acts as an anticoagulant, so species matters [6]. One study reported both mutagenic and antimutagenic behavior of C. lechleri [7].

timeline.event: The Periplus mentions Socotra as a source of dragon's blood [6].
Balfour's Socotra expedition leads to the first formal study of its origin [6].
FDA approves crofelemer (Mytesi), derived from Croton lechleri sap [7].
